a: Moab revolted against Israel
p: One line here, picked up again in 3:4–5, matches the boast of a Moabite king carved in stone.
b: David had made Moab a subject kingdom (2 Samuel 8:2), and after the split of the kingdom it paid tribute to the north. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription found at Dhiban in 1868, says that Omri king of Israel "oppressed Moab many days," and that Mesha threw off Israel's rule (see the notes on 3:4–5 and the chapter 3 page). Kings mentions the revolt here, then leaves it hanging while the story of Ahaziah and Elijah is told, and only comes back to it in chapter 3. The verse also marks a turn: with Ahab dead, the house of Omri begins to lose what it had won.

a: the window screen of his roof room
p: The king falls through a wooden grille, the kind used to shade an upper room's window or roof opening.
b: The Hebrew sevakhah is a net or lattice. The same word is used for the bronze network on the temple pillars (1 Kings 7:17). Here it is most likely a wooden screen over a window or over an opening in the roof of the king's "roof room," the cool upper chamber of a house (compare 1 Kings 17:19). The text does not say how far he fell or how badly he was hurt, only that he "became sick" (vayyachal). The rest of the chapter turns on this bed: he went "up" into it and, Elijah says, he will never come "down."

a: Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron
p: Baal-zebub means "Baal of flies." It may be a Hebrew mockery of the title "Baal the Prince," Baal-zebul.
b: As written, Ba'al zevuv means "lord of flies," and the Greek translators rendered it "Baal Fly" (see the variant). Some think Ekron really worshiped a god who drove away flies or sent oracles through their buzzing. But in the Ugaritic texts Baal is called zbl b'l, "Prince Baal," and many scholars think Israel's writers changed zevul, "prince," to zevuv, "flies," as a sneer, the way Ish-baal became Ish-bosheth, "man of shame." The older form survives in the gospels, where "Beelzebul" is a name for the prince of demons (Mark 3:22; Matthew 12:24).

a: the angel of the LORD
t: The king's messengers and the LORD's messenger
p: The Hebrew uses one word, mal'akh, for the king's messengers and for "the angel of the LORD."
b: Mal'akh means "messenger." When it is the LORD's, English Bibles usually say "angel." The chapter plays on the word: the king sends his mal'akhim to a foreign god (1:2), and the LORD's mal'akh sends Elijah to turn them back (1:3). The king's messengers go and return; the LORD's messenger speaks and is obeyed. "The LORD" in capitals stands for the divine name YHWH, as everywhere on this site. The angel of the LORD appears again in 1:15 and, in this book, only once more, when he strikes the Assyrian camp (19:35).
orig: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (mal'akh YHWH), "the messenger of the LORD"

a: Is it for lack of a God in Israel
p: Three times the same question is asked: is there no God in Israel? The Naaman story answers it from the other side.
b: The angel gives Elijah a question that is repeated word for word in 1:6 and 1:16. Ahaziah is the son of Ahab and Jezebel, who brought Baal into Samaria (1 Kings 16:31–32), and the fight on Mount Carmel over who is God in Israel (1 Kings 18:21, 18:39) is not yet finished. The question comes back in chapter 5 from a foreigner's mouth: Elisha wants Naaman to "know there is a prophet in Israel" (5:8), and Naaman, healed, says "there is no God in all the earth, only in Israel" (5:15). A king of Israel sends abroad to ask about his life; a foreign general comes to Israel and finds it.

a: You will never come down from the bed you went up into
p: The chapter is built on the verbs "go up" and "come down": the king, the fire, the soldiers and the prophet.
b: The Hebrew keeps returning to two verbs. The king "went up" into his bed and will not "come down" (1:4, 1:6, 1:16). Elijah sits on top of a hill; the captains "go up" to him and order, "Come down!" (1:9, 1:11). Instead fire "comes down" out of the sky (1:10, 1:12, 1:14). Only when the LORD's angel tells him does Elijah "go down" (1:15). The next chapter turns the pattern upward: the LORD takes Elijah "up" to the heavens (2:1, 2:11), and boys jeer at Elisha, "Go on up" (2:23). The storyteller uses the words to ask who really has power to raise and lower.

a: He was a hairy man
p: The Hebrew is "a master of hair." It may describe Elijah's body or his coat of hair.
b: Ba'al se'ar is literally "an owner of hair." It can mean a man with long hair and beard (so the KJV, "an hairy man") or a man wearing a garment of hair, which many modern versions prefer. Zechariah 13:4 speaks of prophets wearing "a hairy cloak" to look the part, and Elijah's 'adderet, the cloak he throws over Elisha (1 Kings 19:19) and leaves behind in 2:13, may be such a coat. The leather loincloth shows a man who lives rough. The gospels dress John the Baptist the same way, in camel's hair with a leather belt (Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6), to show him as the Elijah who was to come (Malachi 4:5; Matthew 11:14).
orig: אִישׁ בַּעַל שֵׂעָר ('ish ba'al se'ar), "a man, an owner of hair"
r: Zechariah 13:4; 1 Kings 19:19; 2:13; Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6; Malachi 4:5; Matthew 11:14

a: Man of God
p: In Hebrew "man" ('ish) and "fire" ('esh) sound almost alike. Elijah turns the captain's title into a test.
b: The captain calls Elijah 'ish ha'elohim, "man of God," a common title for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:6; 1 Kings 17:18). He uses it as a form of address while giving orders in the king's name. Elijah answers, "If I am a man of God, then let fire come down" (1:10). In Hebrew the words are close: 'ish, "man," and 'esh, "fire." In 1:12 the narrator even says "the fire of God," 'esh 'elohim, an echo of "man of God." The play makes the point of the story: the title is not a polite word, it is a claim that God stands behind this man.

a: let fire come down out of the sky and devour you and your fifty
p: Readers have long been troubled by the death of two captains and their men. Three ways of reading the scene.
b: As judgment on the king: traditional Jewish and Christian readers see the soldiers as the arm of a king who has rejected the LORD and now tries to seize his prophet by force, as Jezebel tried before (1 Kings 19:2). The fire repeats Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) and shows that the God of Israel answers. As a contrast: the third captain lives because he asks for mercy instead of giving orders (1:13–14), so the story also teaches humility before God. As a hard text: when James and John want to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebukes them (Luke 9:54–55), and many Christian readers take that as a deliberate correction of this scene. Critical scholars often see a prophetic legend that magnifies the prophet's power.

a: the fire of God
p: "Fire of God" can be an idiom for lightning, as in Job 1:16.
b: In Job 1:16 a messenger reports that "the fire of God fell from the sky" and burned up the sheep, which most readers take as lightning. Some commentators read Elijah's fire the same way, a lightning strike from a storm. That does not make the story less of a sign: in the Bible God sends lightning as his own fire (Psalm 18:12–14). The added word "of God" in the second strike, missing from the first, may also be the narrator's way of saying that this time no one can doubt where it came from.

a: He pleaded with him
p: He comes on his knees, not with an order, and asks for his men's lives as well as his own.
b: The first two captains speak for the king: "the king orders you," "the king says this" (1:9, 1:11). The third says nothing about the king. He kneels, pleads (vayyitchannen, the verb for asking a favor), calls his men "your servants," and asks that their lives be "precious" to Elijah. The angel's word "have no fear of him" (1:15) suggests that the danger to Elijah was real. Christian preachers often use the scene to show that God hears those who come humbly, a theme that recalls Ahab's own humbling (1 Kings 21:29).

a: these fifty servants of yours
p: The captain calls his soldiers Elijah's "servants," a polite way of putting himself and his men at the prophet's mercy.
b: The Hebrew 'eved covers everyone from a household slave to a king's high officer, and it is also the normal polite word for oneself before a superior ("your servant"). This site renders it "servant" or "slave" by context. Here the captain gives his soldiers to Elijah as "your servants," the language of a man asking for mercy. The same humble self-reference runs through these chapters: the widow (4:2), the Shunammite as "your servant girl" (4:16), Naaman (5:17–18) and Hazael (8:13).

a: in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat
t: Two Jehorams and a puzzle of dates
p: Here Israel's new king starts in the second year of Judah's Jehoram; in 3:1 it is Jehoshaphat's eighteenth year.
b: For a few years both kingdoms had kings named Jehoram (also spelled Joram), and they were brothers-in-law (8:18). The dates do not line up at first sight. 1:17 puts Jehoram of Israel's start in the second year of Jehoram of Judah, but 3:1 puts it in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, and 8:16 has Jehoram of Judah begin in the fifth year of Jehoram of Israel. The usual answer, worked out by Edwin Thiele and others, is that Jehoram of Judah ruled alongside his father Jehoshaphat for some years, and that the two dates count from different starting points. Others think Kings has two systems of dating side by side. The Greek drops the 1:17 date and instead gives a notice after 1:18 that agrees with 3:1 (see the variants on 1:17 and 1:18).

a: because Ahaziah had no son
p: Ahaziah ruled less than two years. His brother Jehoram, another son of Ahab, follows him.
b: Ahaziah had become king in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat and ruled "two years" (1 Kings 22:51), which by the way Kings counts may mean little more than one. With no son to follow him, the crown passed to his brother Jehoram, "son of Ahab" (3:1). He will be the last king of Omri's house: Jehu kills him at Jezreel in 9:24. So the chapter that opened with Moab breaking away ends with the house of Ahab shrinking, as Elijah had warned (1 Kings 21:21–22).

a: in a windstorm
t: A storm wind, not a chariot
p: Elijah goes up in a se'arah, a storm wind. The fiery chariot separates the two men but is not said to carry him.
b: The Hebrew se'arah is a violent wind, the kind in which God answers Job (Job 38:1) and in which Ezekiel sees God's throne arrive (Ezekiel 1:4). Popular retellings, and songs like "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot," picture Elijah riding the chariot of fire into the sky. The text says that the chariot and horses of fire "came between the two of them," and that "Elijah went up to the heavens in the windstorm" (2:11). The chariot marks the moment and parts teacher from disciple; the storm takes him up.

a: Gilgal
p: They go "down" from Gilgal to Bethel, so this is probably a hill town north of Bethel, not the Gilgal near Jericho.
b: Gilgal, "circle (of stones)," was a common place name. The famous Gilgal is near Jericho by the Jordan, where Israel camped after crossing (Joshua 4:19–20). But in 2:2 the two men "went down to Bethel," and Bethel stands high in the hills, about 2,900 feet up, far above the Jordan valley. So many look for a Gilgal in the hills, and some name Jiljiliya to the north. That site, though, seems to lie lower than Bethel, so it does not solve the problem either, as commentators note. Others take it as the Jordan Gilgal and read "went down" loosely. No answer is certain. Elisha is at a Gilgal again in 4:38.

a: Wait here, please
p: Three times Elijah tells Elisha to stay, and three times Elisha swears he will not leave.
b: The scene repeats three times (2:2, 2:4, 2:6), a storyteller's pattern that builds suspense. It is not clear whether Elijah means to spare Elisha, test him, or go alone. Elisha's oath, "I will never leave you," recalls his promise when he was first called, to follow after Elijah once he had kissed his parents goodbye (1 Kings 19:20–21). Readers have also compared Ruth, who will not leave Naomi though told three times to go back (Ruth 1:8–17). The same oath returns on the lips of the Shunammite woman in 4:30, when she will not leave Elisha.

a: The sons of the prophets
p: "Sons of the prophets" means members of a prophets' community, disciples who lived and worked together under a master.
b: In Hebrew "son of" often means "member of a group." The bene hannevi'im appear in 1 Kings 20:35 and then often around Elisha: at Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal (2:3, 2:5, 4:38), fifty of them at the Jordan (2:7), and a hundred fed at one meal (4:43). They could marry and own debts (4:1), they "sat before" their master to learn (4:38; 6:1), and they did errands for him (9:1). Amos may be distancing himself from such groups when he says, "I am not a prophet, nor a prophet's son" (Amos 7:14). Elijah is called "father" by Elisha (2:12), the title of a guild's head.

a: He struck the water, and the water split apart
t: A new Moses, a new Joshua
p: Elijah parts the Jordan with his cloak, as Moses parted the sea with his staff and Joshua led Israel through the Jordan.
b: The words echo the exodus: the waters "split" (vayyechatsu) and the two cross "on dry ground" (becharavah, as in Exodus 14:21 and Joshua 3:17). The verb for "split" is not the one used of the sea in Exodus 14:21 (baqa'), so the echo rests on the dry ground and on the striking of the water, as Moses lifted his staff over the sea. Elijah crosses back east of the Jordan, into the land where Moses died and was buried in an unknown grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6). Then, like Joshua after Moses, Elisha comes back through the same water to begin his work at Jericho (2:14–22). Many readers see the whole scene as a deliberate retelling: Elijah is a second Moses who leaves the land without a known grave, and Elisha, whose name means "God saves," is a second Joshua, "the LORD saves."

a: his cloak
p: The 'adderet is the same cloak Elijah threw over Elisha at the plow (1 Kings 19:19).
b: 'Adderet is a wide outer cloak, sometimes of hair (Genesis 25:25 compares Esau's hairy body to one). It is Elijah's mark: he covered his face with it at Horeb (1 Kings 19:13) and tossed it onto Elisha to call him (1 Kings 19:19). Here it parts the Jordan, and when it falls from him in 2:13 Elisha picks it up and uses it the same way (2:14). The English phrase "to take up someone's mantle" comes from this scene. The cloak is not magic on its own: Elisha calls on "the LORD, the God of Elijah" as he strikes the water.

a: a double share of your spirit
p: Elisha asks to be Elijah's heir. "A double share" is the inheritance law's portion for a firstborn son, not twice Elijah's power.
b: The Hebrew is pi-shnayim, "a mouth of two," the same phrase Deuteronomy uses for the firstborn son's inheritance: he receives "a double share of everything" his father has (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha is not asking to be twice as great as Elijah, but to be his chief heir among the sons of the prophets. Still, later readers often took it the other way. Ben Sira says Elisha "did twice as many signs" (Sirach 48:12), and a later Jewish tradition counted eight miracles for Elijah and sixteen for Elisha. "Spirit" here is the prophetic gift that the LORD gives (compare Numbers 11:25, where some of the spirit on Moses is put on the elders).

a: If you see me being taken from you
p: Elisha's gift depends on seeing. Seeing what others cannot is a mark of his stories.
b: Elijah does not promise what only God can give; he names a sign. If Elisha sees the moment, he will know the request is granted. And he does see (2:12). Sight runs through the Elisha stories: he sees what Gehazi did far away (5:26) and what the king of Aram says in his bedroom (6:12). He prays that his servant's eyes will be opened to see the fiery army on the hill (6:17), and that the Aramean soldiers will be struck blind and then made to see again (6:18–20). Like the word "seer" for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9), the theme says that a prophet sees what God shows.

a: Elijah went up to the heavens
p: The Bible never tells of Elijah's death. Jewish and Christian readers have drawn different lessons from that.
b: Jewish tradition: like Enoch, who "walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24), Elijah did not die. Malachi promises that God will send Elijah before "the great and terrible day of the LORD" (Malachi 4:5–6), so Jews set a cup for Elijah at the Passover table and a chair for him at every circumcision. Christian readers see Elijah with Moses at the Transfiguration (Mark 9:4) and hear John the Baptist called the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14). Luke tells Jesus' ascension in words that recall this scene: Jesus is "taken up" before his followers' eyes and leaves them his Spirit (Luke 9:51; Acts 1:9–11; Acts 2:1–4). Some interpreters take "the heavens" to mean the sky, not God's dwelling, and note John 3:13.
r: Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; Malachi 4:5–6; Mark 9:4; Matthew 11:14; Luke 9:51; Acts 1:9–11; John 3:13; Sirach 48:9

a: My father! My father! Israel's chariots and riders!
p: Elisha's cry may mean that the prophet, not the chariot force, was Israel's real defense.
b: "Father" is a title for a master prophet (6:21; 13:14), and here it is also the cry of a son at a father's death. "Israel's chariots and riders" is harder. It may describe what Elisha sees, the fiery chariot and horses. But when King Joash weeps over the dying Elisha he says the same words (13:14), and there it can only mean the prophet himself: Elisha was worth more to Israel than its whole chariot corps. The Elisha stories bear that out, for the prophet keeps saving Israel from Aram (6:8–7:20). Some think the title belonged first to Elisha and was later given to Elijah.

a: he gripped his clothes and ripped them into two pieces
t: Claude's theory: one cloak for two pieces
p: My own reading: Elisha tears his own clothes in two and then takes up Elijah's single cloak in their place.
b: This is my own suggestion, built on details others have noticed. Tearing clothes is the normal sign of grief (Genesis 37:34). But the text adds that Elisha tore them "into two pieces," and the very next act is to lift up Elijah's cloak (2:13). Earlier in Kings, the prophet Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces to show a kingdom torn apart (1 Kings 11:30–31). I suggest that the two pieces here show Elisha laying down his old self, and the one cloak shows that he now wears his master's office. Commentators often see the cloak as a sign of succession; reading the torn clothes as part of the same sign is my own proposal.

a: Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?
p: Elisha's question is a call on God to act, like the prayer "Where is the LORD?" that Israel should have asked (Jeremiah 2:6).
b: The question "Where is ...?" is often a cry for God to show himself (Psalm 42:3; Isaiah 63:11). Jeremiah complains that the priests never asked, "Where is the LORD?" (Jeremiah 2:6, 2:8). Elisha's question is the test of his request in 2:9: is the God who answered Elijah now with his heir? The water splits, and the sons of the prophets give the answer in 2:15. In the Greek the question comes after a failure: Elisha strikes once and the water does not part, then asks and strikes again (see the variant).

a: Elijah's spirit has settled on Elisha
p: The prophets see the sign and bow. The handover echoes Moses and Joshua, and later John the Baptist.
b: The verb nachah, "rest, settle," is used when the spirit that was on Moses settled on the seventy elders (Numbers 11:25–26), and Isaiah uses it for the spirit of the LORD resting on the coming king (Isaiah 11:2). Joshua became Moses' successor when Moses laid hands on him and he was "filled with a spirit of wisdom" (Deuteronomy 34:9). The angel tells Zechariah that his son John will "walk ahead of the Lord with Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17). The bow to the ground shows that the guild now accepts Elisha as its head.

a: The LORD's Spirit may have carried him off
p: Ruach means both "wind" and "spirit." The prophets fear that the same storm has dropped Elijah somewhere in the hills.
b: Obadiah once feared exactly this: "the LORD's Spirit will carry you off to who knows where" (1 Kings 18:12). Ezekiel says the Spirit "lifted me up" and carried him (Ezekiel 3:14; 8:3), and in Acts the Spirit snatches Philip away (Acts 8:39). Since the storm wind (se'arah) took Elijah up, the prophets think a wind from the LORD may have set him down again. Elisha knows better, but gives in; the three-day search finds nothing, which confirms that Elijah has truly been taken.
orig: רוּחַ יְהוָה (ruach YHWH), "the wind / Spirit of the LORD"

a: the land causes miscarriages
p: The Hebrew word means "causing loss of children." It may refer to miscarriage in women and animals, or to fruit that drops.
b: Meshakkelet comes from the verb shakhol, which means to lose one's children. Exodus 23:26 promises that "no woman will lose her young or be unable to bear" (Exodus 23:26). Some versions say "barren" or "unfruitful." The spring at Jericho (2:21) may have carried something that caused miscarriage and sickness; E. V. Hulse suggested the parasite of schistosomiasis, carried by water snails. Readers have also linked it to Joshua's curse on whoever rebuilt Jericho, that he would lose his firstborn and his youngest (Joshua 6:26), which came true for Hiel in Ahab's days (1 Kings 16:34). If so, Elisha's first act lifts an old curse from the city.

a: a new bowl and put salt in there
p: An unused bowl was clean; salt stood for purity and for a covenant that lasts.
b: A new vessel had never been used for anything common (compare the new cart in 1 Samuel 6:7). Salt was added to every offering (Leviticus 2:13), and a lasting covenant was called "a covenant of salt" (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5). Newborns were rubbed with salt (Ezekiel 16:4). The salt does not heal the water by itself, since salt makes water worse, and the words are clear: "the LORD says this: I have healed this water" (2:21). The spring at Tell es-Sultan, old Jericho, is still called "Elisha's Spring" (Ain es-Sultan).

a: I have healed this water
p: The first miracle in the land repeats the first miracle after the Sea: bitter water made sweet at Marah.
b: Three days after crossing the sea, Israel found bitter water at Marah. Moses threw a piece of wood into it, the water turned sweet, and the LORD said, "I am the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26). Here, just after crossing the Jordan, Elisha throws salt into bad water and says in the LORD's name, "I have healed (rippi'ti) this water." The pattern continues the Moses and Joshua echoes of 2:8. "To this day" (2:22) is the narrator's note that the spring was still good in his time.

a: some young lads
p: The KJV says "little children." The Hebrew na'arim qetannim can mean boys, but na'ar is also used of young men.
b: Na'ar covers a wide range: a baby (Exodus 2:6), the teenage Joseph at seventeen (Genesis 37:2), Absalom as a grown rebel (2 Samuel 18:5), and soldiers and servants (Gehazi is Elisha's na'ar in 4:12). Qatan means "small" or "young." Solomon calls himself a na'ar qatan when he is already king, "I am only a youngster" (1 Kings 3:7). In 2:24 they are yeladim, "youngsters," another broad word (1 Kings 12:8 uses it for Rehoboam's grown advisers). So the group may have been boys, teenagers or young men; forty-two of them were hurt, which suggests a sizable gang rather than a few small children. The Plain English says "young lads" to keep the range open.

a: "Go on up, baldhead!"
p: "Go up" may mock Elijah's going up to heaven, or simply mean "get lost." Baldness was a mark of shame.
b: The verb 'aleh, "go up," is the same word used for Elijah's ascension (2:11), so many readers hear a jeer: "Go on, disappear like your master!" Others take it as plain contempt, "get out of here." Elisha may have been naturally bald, or shaved as a sign of mourning or of his office. In Israel baldness was a mark of humiliation (Isaiah 3:24; Ezekiel 7:18). The scene is set at Bethel, the town of Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–29), where a prophet of the LORD would not be welcome.
orig: עֲלֵה קֵרֵחַ ('aleh qereach), "go up, bald one"

a: he put a curse on them in the LORD's name
p: One of the hardest stories in the Bible. Readers have answered it in several ways.
b: As judgment: traditional readers stress that the curse is "in the LORD's name" and that God, not Elisha, sends the bears, a covenant curse on a rebellious town (Leviticus 26:21–22). The jeering is aimed at the LORD's prophet in the calf town of Bethel, and the youths may be young men, not toddlers (see the note on 2:23). As warning: many critical scholars read a prophetic legend, told among the prophets' disciples, about the danger of mocking a man of God (compare 1:9–12). As troubling: the rabbis themselves were uneasy. The Talmud says Elisha fell sick for it (Bavli Sotah 47a), and imagines the "lads" as empty of good deeds. Some Christian readers set it beside Jesus' blessing of children (Mark 10:14). The text says the bears "ripped into" forty-two; it does not say all of them died.

a: He left there for Mount Carmel
p: Elisha returns to Elijah's mountain and then to the capital. His stories move among these places.
b: Mount Carmel, the ridge over the Mediterranean near modern Haifa, was the place of Elijah's great contest (1 Kings 18:19–40). Elisha seems to have had a home or retreat there: the Shunammite woman rides to him "at Mount Carmel" (4:25). He also lived in Samaria, the capital (5:3; 6:32). His travels draw a map of the northern kingdom: Jericho and the Jordan, Bethel, Carmel, Shunem, Dothan, Samaria, and even Damascus (8:7). The journey of chapter 2 ends where the kings are, for the next stories bring him before them.

a: Jehoram son of Ahab
p: Israel's king is called Jehoram (Yehoram) here and Joram (Yoram) in chapters 8–9. Both mean "the LORD is high."
b: Hebrew names that begin with the divine name have a long form, Yeho-, and a short form, Yo-. The book uses both for this king: Jehoram in 1:17, 3:1 and 3:6, Joram in 8:16, 8:25 and 8:28–29; chapter 9 uses both (Joram in 9:14 and 9:16, Jehoram in 9:15, 9:17 and 9:21–24). His brother-in-law, the king of Judah, has the same name and is also called by both forms: Jehoram in 1:17, 8:16, 8:25 and 8:29, Joram in 8:21–24. The Plain English follows the Hebrew spelling in each verse. Many modern versions instead call Israel's king "Joram" and Judah's "Jehoram" throughout, which is easier to follow but is an editor's choice. It is striking that Ahab's sons, Ahaziah and Jehoram, both bear names honoring the LORD.

a: He took away the standing stone of Baal that his father had made
p: Jehoram removes one Baal symbol, yet Jehu still finds a Baal temple with standing stones in 10:26–27.
b: A matsevah was an upright stone set up at a shrine as a sign of a god's presence (Genesis 28:18 has Jacob's; Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids them). Ahab had built a temple for Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32), and this stone probably stood there. Jehoram is judged "not like his father and his mother": he did not promote Baal as they did. Yet in 10:26–27 Jehu burns the standing stones of Baal's temple and tears it down, so the cult lived on, perhaps because Jezebel the queen mother still kept it. The Greek has "stones" in the plural in 1:18a and 3:2, and in 1:18a adds that he "broke them."

a: a sheep breeder
p: The Hebrew noqed names a sheep breeder or owner of large flocks. The prophet Amos is called by the same word.
b: Noqed appears only here and in Amos 1:1, where Amos is "among the sheep breeders of Tekoa." In Ugaritic texts the related word names men in charge of the royal herds. The Moabite plateau east of the Dead Sea is rich grazing land, and Moab's wealth was its flocks. Isaiah may remember this tribute when he tells Moab to "send lambs to the ruler of the land" (Isaiah 16:1). The numbers, a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams, are huge, and some think they describe a one-time payment or round figures for a heavy yearly burden.

a: the king of Moab revolted against the king of Israel
p: Mesha's own inscription, found in 1868, tells how he threw off Israel's rule, and names Omri and the LORD.
b: The black basalt stone, about a meter high, was found at Dhiban (biblical Dibon) in Jordan in 1868 and is now in the Louvre. In 34 lines Mesha says: "Omri was king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab many days, for Chemosh was angry with his land. His son followed him, and he too said, 'I will oppress Moab.'" Then Chemosh, Moab's god, "restored" the land in Mesha's days. Mesha took Ataroth, Nebo and Jahaz from Israel, killed their people, and dragged "the vessels of YHWH" before Chemosh. It is the oldest certain mention of Israel's God YHWH outside the Bible (an Egyptian place name "Yhw" is older, but its meaning is debated). The quotations here are summarized from the standard translations.

a: Once Ahab was dead
p: Kings dates the revolt after Ahab's death; the Mesha Stele seems to set it in the days of Omri's "son."
b: The Stele says Omri held Medeba "his days and half the days of his son, forty years." If "son" means Ahab, Mesha was already winning back towns while Ahab lived. Scholars resolve this in several ways. "Son" can mean "grandson," so it may be Jehoram. "Forty years" is a round number for a generation. Mesha may have taken northern towns step by step, beginning under Ahab, while Kings records only the moment he stopped paying tribute (3:4–5). And the war of chapter 3, which ends without Israel retaking Moab, is not mentioned in the Stele at all; Mesha may have carved it before that campaign, or chose not to tell it.

a: I am one with you, my people one with your people, my horses one with your horses
p: Jehoshaphat gives Jehoram the same pledge he gave Ahab before Ramoth-gilead, and again asks for a prophet.
b: The words repeat 1 Kings 22:4 almost exactly, and the scene follows the same pattern: a king of Israel calls on Judah for a war, Jehoshaphat agrees, and then insists on hearing a prophet of the LORD (3:11; 1 Kings 22:5–7). Chronicles has a prophet rebuke Jehoshaphat for helping "those who hate the LORD" (2 Chronicles 19:2), and the alliance ends in failure in both stories. Some scholars think this chapter was shaped to match 1 Kings 22, or even that the king of Judah's name was added to an older story about Israel alone.

a: The road through the wilderness of Edom
p: Instead of crossing the Jordan into Moab's fortified north, the allies march around the Dead Sea to strike from the south.
b: North of the Arnon River, Mesha had fortified towns like Jahaz and Ataroth (the Stele names them). Coming up from the south, through Edom's dry country below the Dead Sea, avoided those forts and brought in Edom as an ally. The road was long: "for seven days they circled around" (3:9). Edom here has a "king," though 1 Kings 22:47 says Edom had only a deputy acting as king in Jehoshaphat's time, under Judah's control. He may be that deputy called by a higher title, or a sign that Edom was already gaining independence, which it wins in 8:20.

a: Oh no!
p: The king's cry, 'ahah, is a groan of despair. He assumes the LORD has trapped them.
b: 'Ahah is a cry of alarm, used by Joshua at Ai (Joshua 7:7) and Gideon before the angel (Judges 6:22). Jehoram does not ask for the LORD's word; he simply assumes the LORD has led them out to die. Jehoshaphat, by contrast, asks for a prophet (3:11). The two kings react to the crisis the way their fathers did before Ramoth-gilead: one looks for any word that suits him, the other for a true word from the LORD (1 Kings 22:7–8).

a: the one who poured water over Elijah's hands
p: Pouring water over a master's hands was a servant's task. The Talmud uses this verse to praise serving a teacher.
b: People washed hands by having water poured over them. The phrase marks Elisha as Elijah's personal attendant, the one who "waited on him" (1 Kings 19:21). The Talmud reasons from this verse that serving a teacher of Torah is greater than studying with him: the verse does not say "who learned from Elijah" but "who poured water on his hands" (Bavli Berakhot 7b). The servant who names him is one of the king of Israel's men, which suggests Elisha was well known at court.
orig: אֲשֶׁר־יָצַק מַיִם עַל־יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ ('asher yatsaq mayim 'al-yede 'Eliyyahu)

a: What is there between you and me?
p: "What to me and to you?" is a Hebrew way to say "This is none of my business" or "Leave me out of it."
b: The idiom mah-li valakh appears when someone refuses a claim or rejects an appeal (Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18). Elisha tells Jehoram to go to "your father's prophets and your mother's prophets," that is, the four hundred who prophesied for Ahab (1 Kings 22:6) and the prophets of Baal and Asherah who ate at Jezebel's table (1 Kings 18:19). The same Greek idiom is used in the gospels, by demons to Jesus (Mark 5:7) and by Jesus to his mother at Cana (John 2:4).
orig: מַה־לִּי וָלָךְ (mah-li valakh), "what to me and to you"
r: Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; 1 Kings 17:18; 1 Kings 18:19; 1 Kings 22:6; John 2:4; Mark 5:7

a: the LORD of Armies
p: YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies." The armies may be Israel's, or the angels, or the stars.
b: This is the first time the title appears in 2 Kings. Tseva'ot means "armies" or "hosts." Some think it first meant Israel's armies (1 Samuel 17:45), others the armies of heaven, angels and stars (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 103:21). Elisha's oath copies Elijah's, "By the life of the LORD of Armies, whom I stand before" (1 Kings 18:15). "Stand before" means to serve, like a courtier before a king. The rendering "the LORD of Armies" is used across this site; the CSB and WEB say much the same.

a: someone who plays the lyre
p: Elisha asks for a musician before he speaks. Music often went with prophecy in Israel.
b: The menaggen is "one who plays strings," the word used for David playing the lyre before Saul (1 Samuel 16:16–23). Saul met a band of prophets coming down with harp, tambourine, flute and lyre, prophesying (1 Samuel 10:5), and David appointed temple singers "to prophesy with lyres" (1 Chronicles 25:1). Elisha may need music to calm himself after his anger at Jehoram, or to open himself to the LORD's word. Prophets elsewhere in the ancient Near East also prophesied in trance states. The Talmud says the spirit of prophecy leaves a prophet who is angry (Bavli Pesahim 66b) and rests only where there is joy, not gloom (Bavli Shabbat 30b), and reads the lyre here as Elisha's way to recover his calm.

a: the LORD's hand came over Elisha
p: The idiom describes the LORD's power seizing a prophet, as when Elijah ran before Ahab (1 Kings 18:46).
b: "The hand of the LORD" on a prophet is a way of describing the moment of inspiration or ecstasy. It gave Elijah strength to outrun Ahab's chariot (1 Kings 18:46), and Ezekiel uses it again and again to introduce his visions (Ezekiel 1:3; 3:14; 8:1; 37:1). The phrase is physical: the prophet feels gripped. What follows in 3:16–19 is the word that Jehoshaphat asked for.

a: Make this wadi into trenches, trench after trench
t: Dig, or the LORD will make pools?
p: The Hebrew can be a command to dig ditches, or a promise that God will fill the wadi with pools.
b: 'Asoh is an infinitive, a form Hebrew uses both for commands and for statements. The KJV and many readers take it as an order: "Make this valley full of ditches." Others, as in some modern versions, read it as the LORD's promise to fill the streambed with pools. Gevim gevim, "pits, pits," means "many pits." A nachal is a wadi, a streambed that is dry most of the year. A flash flood from rain on Edom's mountains, unseen by the army, can fill such a wadi suddenly, and natural explanations of 3:20 are often given. The text's point is that the water comes at the LORD's word and at the hour of the morning offering.
orig: עָשֹׂה הַנַּחַל הַזֶּה גֵּבִים גֵּבִים ('asoh hannachal hazzeh gevim gevim)

a: You will bring down every good tree
p: Deuteronomy forbids cutting down fruit trees in a siege (Deuteronomy 20:19). Here the prophet says Israel will do it.
b: The law says, "do not destroy its trees by swinging an axe against them. You may eat from them, but do not cut them down" (Deuteronomy 20:19). Readers answer the conflict in different ways. Some note that 3:19 is a prediction, not a command: Elisha says what the army "will" do, not what God approves. Others say the law covered only cities inside the promised land, or only trees the army needed for food. Critical scholars often think the prophetic story was older than, or unaware of, Deuteronomy's rule. Assyrian kings boasted of cutting down enemies' orchards, and the scorched-earth war of 3:25 fits ancient practice.

a: about when the grain offering goes up
p: The water arrives at the morning offering, as Elijah's fire fell at the evening offering on Carmel.
b: The law set a lamb and a grain offering every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). In 1 Kings 18:36, Elijah prayed "when the hour came for the grain offering to go up," and fire fell. Here water comes at the same kind of hour. Far from Jerusalem, in the wilderness of Edom, the narrator still keeps time by the temple's worship. The offering hour also links the answer to the prayer of God's people (compare Daniel 9:21; Acts 3:1).

a: red like blood
p: The Hebrew sounds tie together Edom, 'adom "red," and dam "blood." The water from Edom looks like blood.
b: The water comes "by way of Edom" (3:20). Seen across the plain with the sunrise on it, perhaps colored by red earth or sandstone, it looks 'adummim, "red," kaddam, "like blood." The names do the work: Edom means "red" (Genesis 25:30), and dam is "blood." The Moabites conclude the allies have turned on one another, which was not unlikely in an alliance of old enemies. The same water that saved Israel's army lures Moab to its defeat.

a: Kir-hareseth
p: Kir-hareseth is probably Kerak, a fortress on a steep hill above the Dead Sea, still crowned by a Crusader castle.
b: Isaiah and Jeremiah mourn for Kir-hareseth (also Kir-heres) when they lament Moab (Isaiah 16:7, 16:11; Jeremiah 48:31, 48:36). Most identify it with Kerak in Jordan, a natural stronghold where the Crusaders later built a great castle. The Mesha Stele names a royal quarter called Qarhoh at Dibon, which some once linked with it. The "men with slings" could hurl stones far and accurately (Judges 20:16), useful for clearing the walls of defenders.

a: toward the king of Edom
p: Mesha tries to break out at Edom's part of the line, perhaps the weakest, or perhaps to seize Edom's king.
b: The text does not say why Mesha chose Edom's section. It may have been the weakest point, held by an unwilling ally. Some scholars, noting that Edom and Aram look alike in Hebrew letters, suggest the original said "the king of Aram," Moab's possible ally to the north; there is no manuscript for this. Some medieval Jewish commentators, among them Rashi, connected the verse with Amos 2:1, which condemns Moab "because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to lime," and supposed Mesha captured Edom's crown prince and it was he who was sacrificed in 3:27 (see the note there).

a: sacrificed him as a burnt offering on the wall
p: An Ugaritic prayer for a city under attack promises Baal a firstborn. Mesha's act fits a known pattern of last-hope offerings.
b: A ritual text from Ugarit (KTU 1.119, about 1200 BC) tells the people what to pray "when a strong one attacks your gate": they are to promise Baal a bull, a vow, and "a firstborn, O Baal, we will sacrifice." Classical writers say Phoenician cities offered children in disasters, though how often that happened is debated. The Bible knows such offerings and condemns them in Israel (Deuteronomy 12:31; 2 Kings 16:3; 21:6; Micah 6:7), while the stories of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22) and Jephthah's daughter (Judges 11:30–40) circle the same horror. Verdict: a real practice of the region in times of extreme danger; the text reports it without approving it.

a: And there was great wrath upon Israel
p: The Hebrew qetsef almost always means God's anger. But the verse does not say whose wrath fell on Israel, or why.
b: Qetsef, "wrath, fury," is used in the Hebrew Bible mostly for God's anger, often breaking out against Israel (Numbers 1:53; 18:5; Joshua 22:20; 2 Chronicles 19:2). That is the strongest argument that the narrator means a supernatural wrath, not just a human mood. The verse leaves the source open: it says only that "there was" great wrath "upon" or "against" Israel. The Greek translators softened it to "great regret" (see the variant), and the KJV's "great indignation" can sound like a human feeling. The views are set out in the next note and on the chapter page.

a: They pulled away from him and went back to their own land
p: Readers give four main answers, from Chemosh's power to Israel's own horror.
b: Chemosh's wrath: many critical scholars think the old story assumed that Moab's god, moved by the sacrifice, fought for his land, much as the Mesha Stele says Chemosh's anger and favor decided Moab's fate (compare Judges 11:24; 1 Samuel 26:19). The LORD's wrath: others think the narrator means the LORD's anger fell on Israel, for driving a king to such an act, for overreaching the prophecy, or for a sin not named. In the Talmud (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b) two rabbis disagree whether Mesha offered his son to heaven or to an idol; on the first view, the wrath fell on Israel because a foreign king had gone this far for God. Human horror: Josephus says the kings were moved to pity and broke off the siege (Antiquities 9.3.2), and the Greek speaks of "regret." Moab's fury: some read a burst of rage among the defenders that drove Israel back. Either way, Elisha's promise of victory (3:18) came true in the field, but Moab stayed free.

a: the wife of one of the sons of the prophets
p: Jewish tradition and Josephus say she was the widow of Obadiah, who hid a hundred prophets and borrowed to feed them.
b: The text gives no names. But the Targum adds that she was "the wife of Obadiah," and Josephus tells the same story: Obadiah, Ahab's steward, had borrowed money to feed the hundred prophets he hid in caves (1 Kings 18:3–4, 18:13), and after his death the lender came for his sons (Antiquities 9.4.2). Her words "your servant feared the LORD" match Obadiah's own, "your servant has feared the LORD ever since he was a boy" (1 Kings 18:12). The link is a guess, but an old one. The verse also shows that men of the prophets' guilds married and had families.

a: to take my two boys for himself as slaves
p: A lender could take a debtor's children as slaves until the debt was worked off. The law tried to limit it.
b: In Israel, as across the ancient Near East, debts could be paid with labor, and children could be sold or seized (Exodus 21:7; Nehemiah 5:5). The law limited this: a Hebrew debt slave was to go free after six years (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12) and was to be treated like a hired worker, not a slave (Leviticus 25:39–43). The prophets condemned those who sold the poor "for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6). The widow has no legal defense; the lender is within his rights. Elisha does not cancel the debt but gives her the means to pay it.
r: Exodus 21:2–7; Leviticus 25:39–43; Deuteronomy 15:12; Nehemiah 5:5; Amos 2:6; Amos 8:6

a: a small pot of oil
p: The rare word 'asukh probably means a small flask, the kind used for anointing oil.
b: 'Asukh appears only here. It is related to the verb sukh, "to anoint," so it was likely a small vessel for olive oil used on the skin. It shows how little she had: not a storage jar but a flask. Olive oil was food, fuel for lamps and medicine, and it was money: Solomon paid Hiram partly in oil (1 Kings 5:11). Elisha's question "What do you have in the house?" starts from what she already owns.
orig: אָסוּךְ שָׁמֶן ('asukh shamen), "a flask of oil"

a: close the door on yourself and your sons
p: The miracle happens in private, with the door shut, as the raising of the boy will (4:33).
b: Elisha is not present when the oil flows. He sends the woman home to borrow containers and shut the door. In 4:33 he will shut the door on himself and the dead boy before he prays. Jesus, too, raises Jairus' daughter with only a few inside (Mark 5:40). The closed door keeps the miracle from being a show, and it puts the widow and her sons at the center: they do the pouring. How much oil she gets depends on how many containers she gathers.

a: And the oil stood still
p: Elijah fed a widow whose oil did not run out (1 Kings 17:14–16). Elisha's widow pours until there are no more containers.
b: The two stories are close twins. In each a widow is about to lose her sons, by starvation in Zarephath and by slavery here. In each a little oil keeps flowing at a prophet's word. The differences are telling: Elijah's widow is a foreigner who feeds the prophet, Elisha's is an Israelite in debt; one gets a daily supply, the other a fortune to sell. The oil "stood still" (vayya'amod) only when the vessels ran out. Many scholars think stories of one prophet shaped those of the other; others think the narrator paired them on purpose to show Elisha's double share.

a: A woman of standing
p: Hebrew calls her 'ishah gedolah, "a great woman": wealthy and important, and the one who makes the decisions.
b: The phrase describes rank and wealth, as "a great man" does for Naaman (5:1) and Barzillai (2 Samuel 19:32). She is never named. Throughout the story she, not her husband, takes the lead: she invites the prophet, plans the room, refuses favors, rides to Carmel, and later pleads for her land before the king (8:3). Readers have often compared her with Abraham welcoming his three guests (Genesis 18:1–8). Many see her as one of the strongest women in the Hebrew Bible.

a: Shunem
p: Shunem (modern Sulam) lay in the Jezreel Valley, on the slope of the hill of Moreh, near Nain.
b: Shunem guarded the route across the fertile Jezreel Valley. It was the Philistine camp before Saul's last battle (1 Samuel 28:4) and the home of Abishag, who nursed King David (1 Kings 1:3). Mount Carmel, where Elisha stays in 4:25, is 15 to 25 miles to the west, depending on where on the ridge he stayed. Nain, where Jesus raised a widow's son (Luke 7:11–17), lies just across the hill of Moreh, and many readers think Luke means his readers to remember Elisha. Shunem also appears in an Egyptian list of Thutmose III's conquests.

a: a little roof room with walls
p: She builds an upper room with real walls, not just a shelter on the roof, and furnishes it with bed, table, chair and lamp.
b: Flat roofs were used for sleeping in summer, often under a booth. An 'aliyyat-qir, "a roof room of wall," was a permanent upper room, like the one where Elijah stayed at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:19). The four pieces of furniture are a simple guest room: a bed, a table, a seat (kisse', the word for "throne," here a chair) and a lampstand. Christian and Jewish communities have used the phrase "a prophet's chamber" for a room kept for traveling preachers and teachers. The bed is the one on which she will lay her dead son (4:21).

a: I live among my own family
p: Her answer means: "I have my people around me; I need no favors from the court."
b: Elisha offers to speak for her to the king or the army commander, the kind of help a powerful patron could give in a land dispute or a tax matter. Her reply, "among my own people I live," says that her clan protects her. Readers have admired her independence, and the story gives it a twist: years later, after a famine, she will need the king to give back her house and land, and Elisha's servant will be at court to speak for her (8:1–6).

a: she has no son, and her husband is old
t: A son for a childless woman
p: The story follows the Bible's pattern of a childless woman, an old husband, and a promise of a son.
b: Sarah was barren and Abraham old (Genesis 18:11–12); Manoah's wife and Hannah were childless (Judges 13:2; 1 Samuel 1:2). Each time a messenger or prophet announces a son, and the mother doubts or laughs or pleads. Here the woman did not ask for a child, and when it is promised she says, "Don't deceive me" (4:16). In the New Testament, the old priest Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth follow the same pattern (Luke 1:7, 1:13). The pattern says that life in Israel's story is a gift that comes from God, often where hope has ended.

a: At this set time, when the season comes round again
p: Elisha uses the words the LORD spoke to Abraham about Sarah's son (Genesis 18:10, 18:14).
b: The Hebrew phrases lammo'ed hazzeh, "at this set time," and ka'et chayyah, "when the season comes round" (literally "as the time revives"), are the words of Genesis: "At the set time I will come back to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son" (Genesis 18:14). The phrase probably means "a year from now," when the seasons have come full circle. The echo marks the boy as a gift like Isaac, and like Isaac he will be lost and given back (Genesis 22; Hebrews 11:19).
orig: לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה כָּעֵת חַיָּה (lammo'ed hazzeh ka'et chayyah)

a: My head! My head!
p: A child in the harvest fields falls ill with pain in his head and dies by noon, most likely of sunstroke.
b: Grain was harvested in late spring and early summer, when the heat in the Jezreel Valley can be intense. The book of Judith tells of a man who died of heat while overseeing his barley harvest (Judith 8:2–3). Some readers have suggested meningitis or a burst blood vessel. The text gives only the boy's cry and the father's short order. The father's distance is part of the story: he sends the boy away with a servant and later asks his wife why she would go to the prophet (4:23), as if he does not know the child has died.

a: It isn't a new moon or a Sabbath
p: The husband's question shows that people went to see prophets on new moons and Sabbaths.
b: The new moon, the first day of each month, was a holy day with special offerings (Numbers 28:11–15; 1 Samuel 20:5; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13). The verse is one of the early mentions of the Sabbath as a day for visiting a man of God, perhaps to hear teaching or ask for a word. The Talmud draws from it a rule that one should greet one's teacher on a festival (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 16b). Her short reply, shalom, "it is well," hides what has happened (see 4:26).

a: "It is well," she said
p: Her one-word answer, shalom, is the same word as "peace." She will not tell anyone but the prophet.
b: Gehazi asks three times, "Is it shalom with you, with your husband, with the boy?" She answers, "Shalom." She has not lied to her husband or to the servant so much as refused to discuss it with them; she has come for the man of God himself. Readers have heard her word as faith, as grief held in, or as stubborn determination. Horatio Spafford's hymn "It Is Well with My Soul" (1873), written after his four daughters drowned at sea, takes its refrain from this verse in the KJV.

a: The LORD has kept it hidden from me and has not told me
p: Elisha admits he does not know what is wrong. Prophets know only what God shows them.
b: The woman grabs his feet, the posture of someone begging (compare Matthew 28:9; Mark 5:22). Gehazi tries to push her off, but Elisha sees that her soul is "bitter," marah, the word Naomi used of herself (Ruth 1:20). His confession that the LORD has hidden it from him stands against the other stories where he knows what happens in a king's bedroom (6:12) or on the road (5:26). The Bible's prophets are not all-knowing; they see what God reveals, when he reveals it (Amos 3:7).

a: Didn't I tell you, 'Don't lead me on'?
p: She reminds the prophet of her first words. The gift she did not ask for has been taken away.
b: In 4:16 she said, "don't deceive your servant," using the verb kazav, "lie." Now she uses shalah, "mislead, give false hope." She does not say the boy is dead; Elisha understands. Her complaint is like Rachel's cry for children turned on its head (Genesis 30:1), or the widow of Zarephath's charge against Elijah, "You came to me to bring my guilt to mind, and to put my son to death!" (1 Kings 17:18). The Bible lets her speak her anger without rebuke.

a: Whoever you meet, don't say a blessing to him
p: A greeting in Hebrew is a "blessing." Elisha means: go fast and stop for no one.
b: Greetings were long and formal, with blessings asked and returned. The verb is barakh, "bless," used for greeting in 10:15 and in Ruth 2:4. Jesus gives his messengers the same order, "do not greet anybody along the way" (Luke 10:4), and for the same reason: the errand is urgent. "Belt up your clothes" means tuck the long robe into the belt so you can run, as Elijah did before Ahab's chariot (1 Kings 18:46).
orig: לֹא תְבָרְכֶנּוּ (lo tevarekhennu), "do not bless him"

a: there was not a sound, and nobody was listening
p: The staff fails. The words echo Baal's silence on Carmel, when his prophets called and nobody answered.
b: 'En qol ve'en qashev, "no voice and no attention," are almost the words used for Baal at Carmel: "Still not a sound. Not an answer. Nobody was listening" (1 Kings 18:29). Gehazi's attempt with the prophet's staff gets the same result as the Baal prophets' cries. The lesson the storyteller seems to draw is that power does not lie in objects, even a prophet's staff, carried by a servant. Elisha must come himself and pray. Gehazi's failure here also prepares for his greater failure in 5:20–27.
orig: אֵין קוֹל וְאֵין קָשֶׁב ('en qol ve'en qashev)

a: putting his own mouth on the boy's mouth
p: Elisha lies on the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand, as Elijah stretched himself on the widow's son.
b: Elijah stretched himself on the boy at Zarephath three times and cried to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21). Elisha's act is fuller: he matches the boy's body part for part, and the child's flesh warms. Some modern readers think of mouth-to-mouth breathing and suppose the boy was not truly dead. The story itself treats it as a raising of the dead, and it is told as one by the boy's mother, by Gehazi to the king (8:5), and by the writer of Hebrews, who remembers women who "received their dead by resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). Paul at Troas also embraced a young man who had fallen and said, "His life is still in him" (Acts 20:10).

a: The boy sneezed, seven times
p: The verb zarar, "sneeze," appears only here. Seven is the number of completion: the boy is fully alive.
b: The boy's first sign of life is breath, which in Hebrew thinking is life itself (Genesis 2:7). The Greek has no sneezing and makes "seven times" Elisha's crouching over the boy (see the variant). The sneezing shows that breath has returned. Seven stands for completeness in the Bible, and it appears again in the next chapter when Naaman dips seven times in the Jordan (5:14). Elisha's pacing "once this way and once that way" before the second effort may be prayer, or a sign of the struggle.

a: The sons of the prophets were sitting in front of him
p: To "sit before" someone is to be his student or follower, gathered to hear him.
b: Ezekiel says the elders of Judah "were sitting before me" when the word came (Ezekiel 8:1; 14:1), and the people came to sit before him as before a teacher (Ezekiel 33:31). The rabbis later taught, "Let your house be a meeting place for the wise; sit in the dust of their feet" (Mishnah Avot 1:4). The sons of the prophets use the same phrase about their cramped quarters in 6:1. The scene shows a school as well as a commune, with a famine in the background (compare 8:1).

a: wild gourds
p: The paqqu'ot were most likely colocynth, a wild gourd that looks like a small melon but is bitter and toxic.
b: Colocynth (Citrullus colocynthis) grows on sandy ground across the region. Its yellow fruit is round like a small melon and was used in medicine as a strong purge; eaten in quantity it can be deadly. The same word, in the form peqa'im, names the gourd-shaped carvings in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:18; 7:24). A hungry man who did not know the plant would gather them gladly during a famine. The cook's cry "death is in the pot" may describe the bitter taste and the cramps, not deaths.
orig: פַּקֻּעֹת שָׂדֶה (paqqu'ot sadeh), "gourds of the field"

a: Then bring flour
p: As with the salt in 2:20, the flour does not explain the cure. The point is the prophet's word.
b: Flour cannot neutralize a poison, and the text does not say Elisha prayed or spoke the LORD's name. Some readers see a sign-act like the salt at Jericho (2:20–21) and the wood at Marah (Exodus 15:25), where an ordinary thing is the vehicle of God's power. Others, reading the stories as legends of the prophets' guild, see a tale told to honor the master who kept the community alive through famine. Either way the scene shows Elisha caring for his followers' daily needs, not only for kings and armies.

a: firstfruits bread
p: Firstfruits belonged to the priests. This man brings them to the prophet instead.
b: The law gave the first of the grain harvest to the LORD's priests (Numbers 18:12–13; Deuteronomy 18:4). In the north, Jeroboam had appointed priests who were not Levites at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:31). A faithful farmer might bring his firstfruits to the man of God instead. Barley ripened first, so this is spring. The Greek differs here: for karmel, "fresh ears," it has "cakes of figs," and it calls the town Baitharisa. Baal-shalishah was in the hill country of Ephraim, in the "land of Shalishah" where Saul searched for his father's donkeys (1 Samuel 9:4). The gift was meant for Elisha; he gives it to a hundred.

a: For the LORD says this: 'They will eat, and there will be extra.'
p: Twenty loaves feed a hundred men with food to spare. The gospels' feeding stories echo this one.
b: The pattern is the same as in the gospels: a small amount of bread, a servant who protests, a command to give it out, everyone fed, food left over. John's version even has "five barley loaves" and a "boy" who brings them, and after Philip's protest, Andrew asks what that is among so many (John 6:7–9). Mark and Matthew count twelve baskets left over (Mark 6:43; Matthew 14:20). Jesus' feeding of thousands is larger than Elisha's of a hundred, and Christian readers have often taken it as a sign of one "greater than" the prophets (compare Matthew 12:41–42). Moses' manna stands behind both (Exodus 16).

a: because it was through him that the LORD had rescued Aram
p: The narrator says the LORD gave victory to Israel's enemy through Naaman. The God of Israel rules other nations too.
b: Teshu'ah is "rescue, victory," the word used for the LORD's saving acts for Israel (1 Samuel 11:13; 19:5). Here it is Aram's victory, perhaps against Assyria (Aram led the coalition at Qarqar in 853 BC) or even against Israel. The prophets say the same elsewhere: the LORD brought the Arameans from Kir as he brought Israel from Egypt (Amos 9:7), and he can call a foreign king his servant (Isaiah 45:1). Jewish tradition went further and made Naaman the archer who shot Ahab "with no special aim" (1 Kings 22:34); Josephus gives that archer the name Aman (Antiquities 8.15.5), which many take to be Naaman.

a: but he had a skin disease
p: Tsara'at, traditionally "leprosy," is a scaly skin condition, not Hansen's disease. Naaman still led an army.
b: The Hebrew tsara'at covers several conditions that make the skin scaly or flaky, and also mold in cloth and walls (Leviticus 13–14). It does not match the disease now called leprosy, which was probably not known in the region until later. This site renders it "skin disease," following the shared word list. Israel's law kept such people outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46), which is why the four men in 7:3 sit at the gate. Naaman, in Aram, still commands the army and goes in to the king, so his disease does not seem to have shut him out. It is an embarrassment and a burden, the one flaw in a great man.

a: a young girl from the land of Israel
t: A great man and a little girl
p: The story sets the "great man" Naaman against a "little girl," a captive slave, who knows where help is found.
b: Naaman is a "great man" (gadol, 5:1); the girl is a na'arah qetannah, "a little girl." His servants later say, using gadol, "suppose the prophet had given you some big thing to do" (5:13), and when he is healed his flesh is like that of "a young lad," na'ar qaton (5:14). The great man must become like the little ones he had looked past. Robert Cohn and other literary readers have traced this pattern of great and small through the chapter. The girl, torn from her home by raiders, does not curse her captors but wishes her master healed.

a: ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold
p: About 340 kilograms of silver and perhaps 70 kilograms of gold: a fortune by any measure.
b: A talent was about 34 kilograms (75 pounds), so ten talents of silver weighed some 340 kilograms. Omri bought the whole hill of Samaria for two talents (1 Kings 16:24). "Six thousand gold" probably means shekels, at about 11.4 grams each, nearly 70 kilograms. Fine changes of clothes were valued gifts and stores of wealth (Genesis 45:22; Judges 14:12). The size of the gift shows how great Naaman is, and how much he expects healing to cost. Elisha will take none of it (5:16).

a: Am I God, able to kill and make alive
t: Only God kills and makes alive
p: The king's panic quotes the confession that only God holds life and death, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39).
b: Moses' song has the LORD say, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and Hannah sings, "The LORD kills and makes alive" (1 Samuel 2:6). The king of Israel knows this, and he knows that healing tsara'at was thought to be as hard as raising the dead (compare Numbers 12:12). But he does not think of the prophet in his own country. He tears his clothes, the sign of grief or alarm, and suspects a trick to start a war, for Aram and Israel fought often (6:8, 6:24).

a: Then he will know there is a prophet in Israel
p: Elisha's message answers chapter 1's question, "Is it for lack of a God in Israel...?"
b: In chapter 1 a king of Israel sent to a foreign god to ask about his illness, and the LORD asked through Elijah whether there was no God in Israel (1:3). Now a foreigner comes to Israel's king for healing, and the king despairs. Elisha steps in so that the foreigner will learn that there is a prophet in Israel, and through him, God. Naaman's confession in 5:15 completes the thought. The king of Israel is unnamed in this chapter; the story is not about him.

a: Elisha sent a messenger out
p: Elisha does not come out to greet the great man. Naaman takes it as an insult.
b: A general arriving with horses and chariot at a prophet's door expected a reception. Elisha sends a messenger. Some readers see a lesson in humility for the proud Aramean; others see Elisha making sure that the healing is credited to God, not to his own hands. Naaman's anger in 5:11 shows what he expected: a public ritual by the holy man. The cure Elisha prescribes is ordinary washing in an ordinary river, done seven times, the number used in the rite of cleansing for skin disease (Leviticus 14:7).

a: move his hand back and forth over the place
p: Naaman expected a healing rite: the prophet calling on his God and waving his hand over the diseased skin.
b: The verb henif means "to wave, swing," the word used for the wave offering moved before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). Naaman pictures a gesture over "the place," the patch of diseased skin, as healers did. His words show that he already knows the name of "the LORD his God," from the Israelite girl perhaps, but he thinks of Him as a local god whose power works through a holy man's rite. His later request for Israelite soil (5:17) shows the same way of thinking.
orig: וְהֵנִיף יָדוֹ (vehenif yado), "and he will wave his hand"

a: The rivers of Damascus, the Abana and the Pharpar
p: Damascus is an oasis fed by mountain rivers. Next to them the muddy Jordan looked poor.
b: The Abana is usually identified with the Barada, which flows from the Anti-Lebanon mountains through Damascus, and the Pharpar with the Awaj to the south. Their cold, clear water made Damascus a green garden in the desert. The lower Jordan, by contrast, winds through a hot valley and is often brown. Naaman's pride in his homeland is understandable. For the spelling Abana or Amana, see the variant.

a: Father
p: The servants call Naaman "my father." Some scholars think the Hebrew originally read "if," which looks almost the same.
b: The Hebrew 'avi, "my father," is a respectful way for servants to address their master, as the king of Israel calls Elisha "my father" (6:21). But it is unusual from servants, and the Greek has no "my father" at all. So some scholars propose a different small word: 'im or lu, "if," or 'avi read as a rare particle "if only" (compare Job 34:36): "If the prophet had told you some great thing..." Either way the servants' argument is the same: a man ready to do something hard should not refuse something easy. Naaman, to his credit, listens to his servants as he once listened to a slave girl.

a: His flesh came back like the flesh of a young lad, and he was clean
p: Jesus names Naaman as the one healed when Israel's own sick were not (Luke 4:27). Christians saw baptism here.
b: In his sermon at Nazareth Jesus says, "Israel also had many men with skin disease in the prophet Elisha's time, and not one of them was made clean, only Naaman, a Syrian" (Luke 4:27). His point is that God's mercy reaches outsiders, and the crowd is furious. Luke later tells of ten men healed of skin disease, of whom only a Samaritan foreigner returns to give thanks (Luke 17:11–19), as Naaman returns in 5:15. Church fathers, among them Ambrose, read the seven dips in the Jordan as a figure of baptism, where a person is washed and born again "like a little child" (compare John 3:5). The Hebrew na'ar qaton links him to the "little girl" of 5:2.

a: there is no God in all the earth, only in Israel
p: Naaman confesses the God of Israel as the only God. His words echo Rahab and Jethro.
b: Rahab said, "the LORD your God, he is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (Joshua 2:11); Jethro, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods" (Exodus 18:11). Naaman's words go further: there is no God anywhere else. Jewish tradition counts him among the righteous gentiles; the Talmud calls him a ger toshav, a foreigner who accepts the basic laws for all humanity without becoming fully Jewish (Bavli Gittin 57b). Christian readers see in him the first fruits of the gentiles who would come to Israel's God (Isaiah 56:6–7).

a: a blessing
p: Berakhah, "blessing," often means a gift that carries goodwill, as when Jacob urges Esau to accept his present.
b: Jacob begged Esau, "Please take my blessing that has been brought to you" (Genesis 33:11), and Abigail called her gift to David a "blessing" (1 Samuel 25:27). Naaman offers the treasure he brought (5:5) as thanks. In the world of patrons, accepting it would have put Naaman and the prophet into a relationship of exchange. Elisha's refusal keeps the healing a free gift from God.

a: I will not take it
t: A gift that cannot be bought
p: Elisha refuses all payment, as Abram refused the king of Sodom's goods.
b: Prophets could accept gifts (1 Samuel 9:7–8; 1 Kings 14:3; 4:42 here), so the refusal is a choice. Abram swore he would take "not a thread, not a sandal strap" (Genesis 14:23) so no one could say a king made him rich (Genesis 14:22–23). Elisha's oath, "By the life of the LORD, whom I stand before," is the oath of 3:14. Gehazi will soon swear "by the life of the LORD" that he will take something (5:20), and the two oaths frame the second half of the chapter. Jesus told his disciples, "You received for free, so give for free" (Matthew 10:8).

a: a load of soil, as much as two mules can carry
p: Naaman wants Israelite earth so he can worship Israel's God back in Damascus, on the God's own soil.
b: Many in the ancient world thought a god's power was tied to his land. David complained that being driven from Israel was like being told, "Go, serve other gods" (1 Samuel 26:19), and Assyria's settlers in Samaria did not know "the ways of the god of the land" (17:26). The law asked for an altar of earth (Exodus 20:24). Naaman will build one on Israelite soil in Aram. The Greek adds that he asked for some of the "red earth" as well. Some see a new believer's limited understanding; others see a sincere wish to keep worship pure in a foreign land, much as Jews later carried soil from the land of Israel.

a: Rimmon's house
p: Rimmon is Hadad, the storm god of Damascus. His Aramaic title Ramman meant "the thunderer."
b: The great god of Damascus was Hadad, the storm god, also known by the title Ramman, "thunderer" (Akkadian Rammanu). Kings of Damascus took names from him: Ben-hadad, "son of Hadad," and Tabrimmon (1 Kings 15:18). Zechariah 12:11 mentions mourning for "Hadad-rimmon." The Hebrew vowels make the name Rimmon, "pomegranate," which may be a mocking pun. The temple of Hadad stood where the Roman temple of Jupiter and later the Umayyad Mosque were built in Damascus.

a: When I bow down in Rimmon's house, may the LORD forgive your servant in this matter
p: Naaman asks pardon in advance for bowing beside his king in a pagan temple. Readers have long argued about Elisha's answer.
b: Naaman's duty was to support the king on his hand as he bowed, which meant bowing with him. Some take the verbs as past ("when I have bowed"), a confession, but most read them as future. Permission: many Jewish and Christian readers take Elisha's "Go in peace" (5:19) as allowing an outward act that Naaman's heart did not mean. The Talmud draws from this verse that a non-Jew, though forbidden to worship idols, is not commanded to give his life rather than perform an outward act under compulsion, and it reads "Go in peace" as approval on that basis (Bavli Sanhedrin 74b–75a). No ruling: others say "Go in peace" is simply goodbye, leaving the matter to God. A warning: in the Reformation, writers argued whether Naaman's case excused Protestants who still attended Catholic Mass, and many said it did not, since Naaman asked pardon, not approval.

a: "Go in peace," Elisha told him
p: "Go in peace" is a normal farewell, also used when someone is sent off with blessing or approval.
b: Jethro sends Moses off with "Go in peace" (Exodus 4:18), and Eli blesses Hannah with it (1 Samuel 1:17). In those places it carries goodwill and a measure of approval. Whether it answers Naaman's question is debated (see the note on 5:18). Jesus uses the same words to send away people he has healed or forgiven (Mark 5:34; Luke 7:50).

a: the Aramean
p: Gehazi thinks a foreigner should pay. His oath by the LORD copies his master's, to the opposite end.
b: "This Naaman, the Aramean" is said with contempt: why should an enemy general walk away free? Gehazi swears "by the life of the LORD," the oath Elisha used to refuse the gift (5:16), to get some of it. He lies to Naaman (5:22), hides the silver (5:24), and lies to Elisha (5:25). The Mishnah names Gehazi among the four commoners who have no share in the world to come, with Balaam, Doeg and Ahithophel (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). Christian readers often compare Judas, who also served a master and loved money (John 12:6).

a: At the hill
p: The Hebrew 'ofel is a fortified rise or citadel. In Samaria it may be the hill of the royal quarter, near Elisha's house.
b: 'Ofel means a swelling, a mound, and in Jerusalem it names the walled ridge between the City of David and the temple (2 Chronicles 27:3; Nehemiah 3:26). Here it is the point where Gehazi, near home, takes the bags and sends Naaman's servants back, so they will not be seen at Elisha's door. The details show careful planning, which makes the lie worse.

a: Wasn't my heart there with you
p: Elisha says his heart, meaning his mind, went with Gehazi. He saw what happened on the road.
b: In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and knowing, not only feeling. "Did my heart not go?" means "Was I not there in mind?" Elisha's list, "olive groves and vineyards, flocks and herds, servants," names what Gehazi meant to buy with the silver: land and wealth for a comfortable life. The list sounds like Samuel's warning of what a king would take (1 Samuel 8:14–17). The time was wrong: Elisha had refused payment so that the God of Israel's grace would be plain to a foreigner.
orig: לֹא־לִבִּי הָלַךְ (lo-libbi halakh), "did my heart not go?"

a: with skin disease, like snow
p: Most versions say "white as snow." The Hebrew says only "like snow," probably describing flaking skin.
b: Skin disease is "like snow" also for Moses' hand (Exodus 4:6) and Miriam (Numbers 12:10). The comparison may be to the color, but tsara'at is often a scaly, flaking condition, and snow in the Bible is also flakes falling (Psalm 147:16). Gehazi takes on Naaman's disease, and the healed foreigner and the cursed Israelite trade places. Yet in 8:4–5 Gehazi is talking with the king, which suggests either that the stories are not in time order or that his disease did not bar him from court.

a: the place where we sit before you has gotten too cramped for us
p: The prophets' guild has outgrown its meeting place. They build a new one by the Jordan, near Jericho.
b: The guild near Jericho (2:5, 2:15) was big enough to send out fifty men (2:16). Now it needs a larger place "to sit," that is, to meet or to live. They will cut the beams themselves, so the building was probably a simple shelter of poles and mud by the river, where trees grow thick in the Jordan's jungle-like valley (Jeremiah 12:5 speaks of "the thickets of the Jordan"). The sons of the prophets were not rich; one of them has to borrow his ax head (6:5).

a: the iron dropped off into the water
p: Iron tools were expensive in Iron Age Israel. Losing a borrowed ax head could mean a debt the man could not pay.
b: Iron came into common use in the land only gradually, and in Saul's time Israelites had to go to the Philistines to sharpen their tools (1 Samuel 13:19–22). An iron ax head was worth a good deal. The law made a borrower pay for what he borrowed if it was lost or damaged (Exodus 22:14). For a poor member of the guild, this could lead to the kind of debt that threatened the widow's sons in 4:1. The story is small, but it is not trivial to the man who cries out.

a: set the iron floating
p: Miracle, folk tale or sign? Readers have taken this little story in very different ways.
b: A miracle: traditional readers take it as it stands, a sign that God cares for the needs of the poor, even a lost tool. A sign of the cross: Justin Martyr saw in the wood thrown into the Jordan a picture of the cross, by which those sunk in sin are raised up (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 86). A rational explanation: some modern readers suggest that Elisha poked the stick into the socket of the ax head and lifted it, though the verb vayyatsef means "he made it float." A guild legend: critical scholars see one of the short wonder stories, like 2:19–22 and 4:38–41, told among the prophets' disciples to honor their master.

a: I'll make camp at such-and-such a spot
p: The Hebrew word tachanoti, "my camp," is unusual. Many scholars restore a word for "hide" or "lie in ambush."
b: The form tachanoti appears only here and is hard to explain as "my encampment." A small change gives techavu, "you will hide," or a word for an ambush, which fits the next verse, where Aram is "heading down" (nechittim, possibly also "lying hidden") at that place. Either way the king of Aram is setting traps for Israel's king on his own roads, and Elisha keeps warning him. "Such-and-such a spot" is the Hebrew peloni 'almoni, used when a name is left out on purpose (Ruth 4:1).

a: even what you say in the room where you sleep
p: Nothing is hidden from the prophet. Ecclesiastes warns that even bedroom words get out.
b: "Not even in your thoughts should you curse a king, and not even in your bedroom curse someone rich, for a bird of the sky will carry off the sound" (Ecclesiastes 10:20). Here the "bird" is a prophet in Israel. The Aramean king suspects a traitor; his officer knows it is Elisha. The words show how well known Elisha's power was even abroad, which explains why the king sends an army after one man (6:14). Christian readers have compared Jesus' words that nothing hidden will not be made known (Luke 12:2–3).

a: in Dothan
p: Dothan stood on a hill about ten miles north of Samaria, on the road through the hills. Joseph was sold there.
b: Tell Dothan was excavated in the 1950s by Joseph Free and shows a walled town in the Iron Age. It sat beside a pass from the Jezreel Valley to the hills of Samaria, on a trade route: that is why the Ishmaelite caravan that bought Joseph passed by (Genesis 37:17, 37:25). An army could surround it easily, since it stood alone on a mound. Elisha leads the blinded soldiers from there to Samaria, a march of several hours.

a: There are more with us than with them
p: Elisha's word comes back on Hezekiah's lips before Sennacherib, and in the New Testament.
b: When the Assyrians threaten Jerusalem, Hezekiah tells his people, "The one with us is greater than the one with him" (2 Chronicles 32:7); the Hebrew word for "greater" is Elisha's word for "more" (rab), here in the singular. Isaiah's words of 2 Kings 19 make the same point. The New Testament speaks the same way: "If God is for us, who is against us?" (Romans 8:31), and "the one in you is greater than the one in the world" (1 John 4:4, fresh rendering). Elisha does not say how many are with him; he lets his servant see (6:17).

a: the hill was filled with horses and fiery chariots, surrounding Elisha
p: The same horses and chariots of fire that took Elijah now guard Elisha. The LORD's army is unseen until God opens eyes.
b: The fiery chariots recall 2:11–12. Israel's poets describe God's chariots as "tens of thousands" (Psalm 68:17) and his angel camping around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7). Jacob met angels and called the place "a camp of God" (Genesis 32:2) before facing Esau (Genesis 32:1–2), and Jesus told Peter he could call more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). The scene answers 2:12, where Elisha called his master "Israel's chariots and riders": the real chariots of Israel are the LORD's.

a: open his eyes, please, and let him see
p: The LORD opens eyes twice in this story: the servant's, to see the unseen army, and the enemies', to see where they are.
b: Balaam's eyes were "uncovered" to see the angel in his road (Numbers 22:31), and Hagar's eyes were opened to see a well (Genesis 21:19). In this chapter the LORD opens the servant's eyes (6:17), strikes the enemy blind (6:18), and opens their eyes again inside Samaria (6:20). Luke uses the same picture when the two disciples at Emmaus have their eyes opened to know the risen Jesus (Luke 24:31). Seeing is a gift from God in the Elisha stories (see the note on 2:10).

a: Strike this nation blind, please
p: The rare word sanverim is used only here and for the men of Sodom. It means a dazzled confusion, not ordinary blindness.
b: Sanverim appears only here and in Genesis 19:11, where the angels strike the men at Lot's door so they cannot find the door. The soldiers in Dothan can still walk and follow Elisha, so the word seems to mean a confusion of sight in which they cannot recognize where they are or whom they are facing. It may be a borrowed word, perhaps related to Akkadian shunwurum, "very bright," that is, dazzled. The prayer is answered "as Elisha had said."

a: You're on the wrong road
