p: He tells the soldiers this is the wrong town and leads them to Samaria. Readers have debated whether he deceived them.
b: Some readers say Elisha spoke the strict truth: once he left Dothan with them, it was no longer the town where he was, and he did bring them to "the man you're hunting for," himself, in Samaria. Others say this was a lawful trick of war, like the Hebrew midwives' answer to Pharaoh (Exodus 1:19) or Rahab's hiding of the spies (Joshua 2:4–6), which the Bible does not condemn. The result is mercy: no one dies, the captives are fed and sent home (6:22–23). The ruse saves lives on both sides.

a: my father
p: Israel's king, eager to kill the captives, asks Elisha's leave and calls him "my father."
b: The title marks Elisha as a figure of authority to the king, as Elijah was to Elisha (2:12) and Elisha will be to Joash (13:14). The repeated question "Do I cut them down?" shows the king's eagerness. Elisha's answer rests on the law of war as people then understood it: one did not kill prisoners taken alive, and here the LORD, not the king's sword, captured them. Compare the king of Israel's mercy to Ben-hadad in 1 Kings 20:31–34, which a prophet condemned; here the prophet himself commands mercy.

a: Put food and water before them
p: Elisha's order looks ahead to Proverbs and to Paul: if your enemy is hungry, give him bread.
b: "If someone who hates you is hungry, feed him bread, / and if he is thirsty, hand him water to drink" (Proverbs 25:21), which Paul quotes in Romans 12:20. In 2 Chronicles 28:15 the men of Samaria clothe, feed and send home captives from Judah at a prophet's word. The king does more than feed them; he "threw a big feast," vayyikreh kerah gedolah, a rare phrase in which verb and noun share a root. The result is peace for a time (6:23). Jesus' "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44) has often been read with this story.

a: After that, Aram's raiding parties stopped coming into the land of Israel
p: The raids stop, yet the next verse has Ben-hadad besieging Samaria. The stories may come from different times.
b: The raids stopped, but a full invasion follows in 6:24. Some readers see no conflict: small raiding bands ceased, but a royal campaign came later. Others think the Elisha stories were once separate tales, collected without a strict time order, and that "Ben-hadad" in 6:24 is a different king from the one in the raids (see the note on 6:24). The kings of Israel in 6:8–7:20 are never named, which also suggests stories handed down without royal names and later placed in Jehoram's reign.

a: Ben-hadad king of Aram
p: Ben-hadad means "son of Hadad." The Assyrians knew the king of Damascus in these years as Hadad-ezer.
b: Kings names three or more rulers of Damascus as Ben-hadad (1 Kings 15:18; 1 Kings 20:1; 2 Kings 13:3). Assyrian records of Shalmaneser III name the king of Damascus who fought him at Qarqar in 853 BC and after as Adad-idri, that is, Hadad-ezer, and then Hazael (see the note on 8:15). So either "Ben-hadad" was a throne name or title of Hadad-ezer, or these stories first belonged to a later time, when Ben-hadad son of Hazael pressed Israel hard (13:3, 13:24–25). J. Maxwell Miller argued that many of the Aramean war stories in 1 Kings 20–2 Kings 8 originally belonged to the Jehu dynasty.

a: the price of a donkey's head was eighty pieces of silver
p: A donkey was unclean, and its head the poorest part. Eighty silver pieces for it shows how desperate the city was.
b: The donkey is not a clean animal (Leviticus 11:3–7), and its head has little meat. Eighty shekels was a huge price; Jeremiah bought a field for seventeen (Jeremiah 32:9). A quarter kab was about a third of a liter, a little more than a cup. Ancient writers record similar prices in sieges: Assyrian texts describe famine in besieged Babylon, and Josephus tells of the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, where people gathered wild plants and ate leather (Jewish War 5.10.3; 6.3.3). The Greek gives the price as fifty shekels (see the variant). After the siege lifts, a whole seah of fine flour costs one shekel (7:1).

a: If the LORD won't rescue you
p: The Hebrew 'al-yoshi'ekh YHWH can mean "if the LORD does not save you" or "may the LORD not save you!"
b: The negative 'al usually goes with a wish or command, so the words could be a bitter curse: "Let the LORD not save you!" Most read it as a refusal: "If the LORD will not help you, how can I?" The threshing floor and winepress are empty; there is no grain or wine to give. The king's words show his helplessness, and perhaps his anger at the LORD (6:33). Then he asks the woman what is wrong, and she tells him something worse than he imagined.

a: We'll eat him today, and my son we'll eat tomorrow
p: The covenant curses warned that a siege would drive parents to eat their children. Here it happens.
b: Deuteronomy warned that "you will eat your own children" in a siege, and that even the gentlest woman would hide what she ate from her family (Deuteronomy 28:53–57; Leviticus 26:29). Lamentations says it happened when Babylon besieged Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10), and Ezekiel threatened it (Ezekiel 5:10). Assyrian treaties of the seventh century BC name the same horror among the curses on those who break them, and Josephus tells of a mother who ate her child in the Roman siege of Jerusalem (Jewish War 6.3.4). The narrator does not linger; he reports the woman's words and the king's response.

a: "What is it?" the king asked her
p: The scene mirrors Solomon's judgment between two mothers. Solomon could judge; this king can only tear his clothes.
b: In 1 Kings 3:16–28 two women come to King Solomon over two babies, one living and one dead. The true mother pleads for her son's life, and Solomon's wisdom shows who she is: "Give the live child to her. Do not kill him" (1 Kings 3:27). Here two women again bring a case about two sons to a king of Israel. But one son has already been eaten, and the complaint is that the other mother broke her bargain. There is no wise judgment to give. The contrast shows how far the kingdom has fallen since Solomon.

a: sackcloth was underneath, against his skin
p: Under his robes the king wears sackcloth, a sign of mourning or repentance. Yet in the next breath he vows to kill Elisha.
b: Sackcloth was rough goat-hair cloth worn in grief, fasting and repentance (Genesis 37:34; Jonah 3:6). His father Ahab put it on when Elijah condemned him (1 Kings 21:27). The king's sackcloth may show real sorrow before the LORD; or it may be a show of piety while he blames the prophet. Some readers think the king blamed Elisha for urging him to hold out, perhaps with a promise of rescue, while the city starved. The text lets both sides stand: private grief and public rage.

a: This son of a murderer
p: The phrase can mean "this murderer," or it can point to the king's father Ahab, who had Naboth killed.
b: In Hebrew "son of" often means "a person of that kind": "a son of death" is a man condemned (1 Samuel 20:31). So ben-hamratseach may simply mean "this murderer." But the king is Ahab's son, and Ahab was the man Elijah accused: "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" (1 Kings 21:19). Elisha's words may be pointed: like father, like son. "His master's footsteps" tells the elders that the king himself is coming behind his messenger (see 6:33 and 7:2).

a: Why keep hoping in the LORD any longer?
p: The speaker blames the LORD for the famine and sees no reason to wait for him.
b: Yachal, "wait, hope," is the verb of the psalms of trust (Psalm 130:5–7). Here it is turned upside down: if this disaster is the LORD's doing, why go on waiting for him? Some readers think Elisha had told the king to hold out and wait for the LORD's help, which would explain both the sackcloth and the anger. Elisha's answer comes at once in 7:1, a promise for the very next day.

a: one seah of fine flour will cost a shekel, and two seahs of barley a shekel
t: From famine prices to market prices
p: A seah was about seven to twelve liters. The promise means food will be cheap again by tomorrow.
b: Estimates of the seah range from about seven to about twelve liters (two to three gallons). A shekel was a weight of silver, about 11.4 grams. The prices are those of a normal market, perhaps a little high, but after a donkey's head for eighty shekels (6:25) they sound like a dream. Barley was the poor man's grain, half the price of fine wheat flour. "In Samaria's gate" is where the market met. The promise is exact in time, place and price, so that its fulfillment can be checked (7:16–18).

a: The officer whose hand the king leaned on
p: The shalish was the third man in a chariot, and then a senior officer or aide. The king leans on his arm, as Naaman's master did.
b: Shalish is related to "three"; Egyptian chariots carried two men, but Hittite and later Assyrian chariots carried a driver, a fighter and a shield-bearer, and the title came to mean a high officer (Exodus 14:7; 9:25; 15:25). Leaning on a man's arm was a mark of trust and rank, the same picture as Naaman's master in Rimmon's temple (5:18). This officer's scorn for Elisha's word costs him his life (7:17–20). The narrator tells the story twice, in 7:2 and 7:19, to stress that the prophet's word is exact.

a: suppose the LORD were to make windows in the sky
p: The officer mocks: even if the LORD opened the flood windows, flour could not fall that fast.
b: In the flood story "the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11), and in Malachi the LORD promises to "open the windows of heaven" and pour out blessing (Malachi 3:10). The officer's sneer pictures God raining grain from above, as he once rained manna (Exodus 16:4). Elisha does not argue. The answer will come not from the sky but from an empty enemy camp. Like Zechariah, who doubted the angel's word and was struck mute (Luke 1:20), the officer will see the promise kept but not share in it.

a: four men with skin disease
p: The law kept people with skin disease outside the camp. Jewish tradition said these four were Gehazi and his sons.
b: Leviticus says of a person with tsara'at, "He is to live alone, and his home is to be outside the camp" (Leviticus 13:46; compare Numbers 5:2–3). In a walled city that meant outside the gate, where these four men waited on charity that no longer came. The Talmud, linking this chapter to the curse on Gehazi and his descendants in 5:27, says the four were Gehazi and his three sons (Bavli Sotah 47a; Bavli Sanhedrin 107b). The text names no one. The outcasts, not the king or the army, discover the rescue and bring the good news.

a: let's desert to Aram's camp
p: The Hebrew "fall to" means to go over to the enemy, to surrender or desert.
b: Nippelah 'el, "let us fall to," is the idiom for deserting to the other side (1 Chronicles 12:19–20; Jeremiah 21:9; 37:13–14). Jeremiah would later advise Jerusalem's people to "fall to" the Babylonians to save their lives (Jeremiah 21:9), and was accused of doing it himself. The men's logic is cold and clear: inside or outside, they will die anyway; the enemy is their only chance.

a: The Lord had let Aram's camp hear a noise
p: The Lord routs Aram with a noise alone. Here the Hebrew has Adonai, "the Lord," not the divine name.
b: The text here uses 'Adonai, "the Lord," written in small letters on this site, instead of YHWH, "the LORD." The rescue is like others in Israel's story: the sound of marching in the treetops before David attacked the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:24), the panic the LORD threw into Egypt's army (Exodus 14:24–25), Gideon's trumpets and torches (Judges 7:19–22). The Arameans hear what Elisha's servant saw in 6:17, the army of heaven, and they flee from it.

a: the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt
p: By this time the Hittite empire was long gone, but "Hittite" kingdoms ruled north Syria. Egypt may be Musri, a land to the north.
b: After the Hittite empire fell (about 1180 BC), small "Neo-Hittite" kingdoms such as Carchemish and Hamath held north Syria, and Assyrian records call the whole region "the land of Hatti." Egypt in the 9th century was weak and divided, so some scholars think the Hebrew Mitsrayim here, as perhaps in 1 Kings 10:28–29, once meant Musri, a land in southeastern Anatolia (Cilicia) known from Assyrian texts. Others keep Egypt, since the Arameans' fear did not need to be realistic: they panicked at the sound.

a: Today is a day of good news
p: Besorah, "good news," is the word behind the Greek euangelion, "gospel." Silence would be a sin.
b: The noun besorah and the verb bisser, "bring good news," are used for news of victory (1 Samuel 31:9; 2 Samuel 18:19–27). Isaiah uses them for the messenger who announces that God reigns (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7), and the Greek translation of those verses gave the New Testament its word "gospel." Christian preachers have often used the lepers' words, "we're sitting on it," as a call to share good news. In the story the men's motive is also fear: "guilt will find us out," that is, punishment will catch up with them.

a: They know that we're hungry
p: The king thinks the empty camp is an ambush, a trick Joshua once used at Ai.
b: Pretending to flee and then ambushing the enemy was a known tactic: Joshua took Ai that way (Joshua 8:3–22), and Israel did it against Gibeah (Judges 20:29–36). The king's caution is reasonable. But it also shows the same unbelief as his officer's (7:2): he does not think of Elisha's promise. His servant's plan, to risk a few horses that will die anyway, wins the day.

a: two chariot teams
p: The Hebrew "two chariots of horses" is unusual. The point is a small scouting party.
b: The officer suggested five horses (7:13); the king sends "two chariots, horses," perhaps two chariots with their teams. The Greek seems to understand two mounted riders. Either way the party is small, and the king calls them "messengers" in 7:15. They follow the trail all the way to the Jordan, about twenty-five miles east, the road home to Damascus.

a: The crowd ran over him in the gateway and he died
t: The word comes true to the letter
p: The officer who mocked the promise sees the cheap flour and is crushed by the crowd rushing to buy it.
b: The king put the doubting officer at the gate, perhaps to keep order as the starving people rushed out to the camp and back with food. He saw the promise kept and did not eat of it, exactly as Elisha said (7:2). The narrator then repeats the prophecy and the officer's taunt in full (7:18–20). This kind of retelling, "as the LORD's word had said," is a mark of Kings, which keeps showing prophecies fulfilled (1 Kings 15:29; 16:34; 22:38). Gerhard von Rad called it the book's theology of the word.

a: The LORD has summoned a famine
p: The LORD "calls" the famine like a servant summoned to work. Seven years recalls Joseph's Egypt.
b: The verb qara', "call, summon," is used of God calling a famine in Psalm 105:16 ("he called a famine down on the land") and a drought in Haggai 1:11. Seven years of famine come in Joseph's day (Genesis 41:27) and are offered to David as a punishment (2 Samuel 24:13, where Chronicles has three). The flashback (Elisha "had talked" with her) ties this story to 4:8–37: the prophet who gave her a son now saves her household again. Some think this is the famine of 4:38.

a: lived as foreigners in Philistine country
p: Like Elimelech's family, who went to Moab in a famine, she goes abroad to survive.
b: Famine sent Abraham to Egypt (Genesis 12:10), Isaac to the Philistine town of Gerar (Genesis 26:1), Jacob's sons to Egypt (Genesis 42), and Naomi's family to Moab (Ruth 1:1). Each time the family "lived as foreigners" (gur), without land rights. The Philistine coastal plain, watered by winter rains from the sea, may have been spared the worst. Like Naomi, the woman comes back after the famine to find her land in other hands (Ruth 4:3).

a: She went to plead with the king for her house and her field
p: Land left empty could be taken by the crown or by neighbors. She must appeal to the king to get it back.
b: Ancient law codes dealt with fields left behind. The Code of Hammurabi says that if a soldier leaves his field and another man farms it for three years, the land passes to the one who worked it, though a short absence did not cost the owner his land (laws 30–31). In Israel the king may have taken abandoned fields, as Ahab seized Naboth's vineyard after his death (1 Kings 21:15–16). The woman who once said "I live among my own family" (4:13) now needs the king's word.

a: Gehazi, the man of God's servant
p: After 5:27 we expect Gehazi to be shut out by skin disease. Here he chats with the king. Readers explain it in several ways.
b: Not in time order: the Elisha stories may be grouped by theme, and this scene may come from before chapter 5. The flashback form, "Elisha had talked" (8:1), supports this. Still at court: others note that skin disease did not keep Naaman from his king (5:1), and in Israel a man might talk with the king outdoors. No repentance: the best-known tradition says Elisha went to Damascus to bring Gehazi back, but Gehazi would not repent (Bavli Sotah 47a; Bavli Sanhedrin 107b), so others read this scene as earlier than 5:27. The king here wants to hear "all the great things Elisha has done," which shows how famous the prophet had become.

a: Gehazi was in the middle of telling the king
p: Just as Gehazi tells of the raised boy, the boy and his mother walk in. The narrator lets the timing speak for God.
b: The text says nothing about God here, but the coincidence is the point. Similar timing turns the Esther story: the king cannot sleep, hears the record of Mordecai's good deed, and Haman walks in at that moment (Esther 6:1–4). Ruth "happened" to come to Boaz's field (Ruth 2:3). Readers in the Jewish and Christian traditions alike have seen such moments as the hidden hand of God, which the Hebrew Bible often shows without naming.

a: all that her field has produced
p: The king gives her the land and all its harvest since she left, a full restoration.
b: A saris, here "official," was a court officer, sometimes a eunuch (the word can mean either). The king's order goes beyond justice: she receives not only the land but its produce for seven years. The king in this story is unnamed, like the king of Israel throughout chapters 5–7. Some readers think he is Jehoram; others, Jehu or a later king, since the stories are not in time order.

a: Elisha went to Damascus
p: At Horeb Elijah was told to anoint Hazael king of Aram. Elisha now goes to Damascus and names him.
b: At Horeb the LORD gave Elijah three tasks: anoint Hazael king over Aram, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha as prophet (1 Kings 19:15–16). Elijah called Elisha, but the other two fall to his heir. Elisha does not pour oil on Hazael; he tells him what he will become (8:13). In the next chapter he sends a disciple to anoint Jehu (9:1–3). The Hebrew for "anoint" never appears in this scene, which has led some to say the command was carried out in a different way, by a prophetic word.

a: enough to load forty camels
p: Forty camel loads of the best of Damascus: a king's gift to a famous foreign prophet.
b: Damascus sat on the great trade routes from Mesopotamia and Arabia, and its markets were rich (Ezekiel 27:18). Forty may be a round number for "a great many." The gift contrasts with Naaman's, which Elisha refused (5:16); the text does not say whether he took this one. The sick Ben-hadad calls himself Elisha's "son," a term of deep respect for a superior, like Ahaz's "your servant and your son" to the king of Assyria (16:7).

a: But the LORD has shown me he is sure to die
p: Elisha says to tell the king he will live, yet he will die. Did the prophet tell Hazael to lie?
b: The verse can be read several ways. The illness is not fatal: Ben-hadad would recover from his sickness, but he will die by another cause, Hazael's hand (8:15). Hazael's lie: Elisha tells Hazael what he will in fact say, foreseeing his deceit. The written text: the Ketiv reads "Go, say: you will not live," with no lie at all (see the variant). Most versions follow the spoken reading. The question of whether a prophet may deliver a misleading word recalls Micaiah's vision in 1 Kings 22:19–23.

a: until he was ashamed
p: Elisha stares at Hazael until "he" is ashamed. It may be Hazael, uneasy under the gaze, or Elisha himself.
b: The Hebrew has no names: "he made his face stand and set it, until shame." Most take it that Elisha fixed his eyes on Hazael until Hazael grew uncomfortable, as if Elisha could read his plans. Others think Elisha stared until he himself felt ashamed, then wept. The same phrase "until shame" was used in 2:17 for the sons of the prophets pressing Elisha. The man of God weeps because he sees what is coming for Israel (8:12).

a: Their little ones you will smash, and their pregnant women you will slash open
p: Hazael became Israel's worst enemy. Kings and Amos both record the cruelty of his campaigns.
b: Under Hazael, Aram took all of Israel's land east of the Jordan (10:32–33), struck down Jehoahaz's army until it was "like dust at threshing" (13:7), and even threatened Jerusalem (12:17–18). Amos condemns Damascus "because they threshed Gilead with iron sledges" (Amos 1:3–4). Slaughtering children and ripping open pregnant women were the horrors of ancient war (Hosea 13:16; Amos 1:13; 15:16 here). Elisha weeps as a prophet who loves the people his word condemns, as Jeremiah later would (Jeremiah 9:1).

a: Your servant is just a dog
p: Calling oneself a dog was a polite way to say "I am nobody." The Lachish letters use the same phrase.
b: David asks Saul, "Who is it you are chasing? A dead dog" (1 Samuel 24:14), and Mephibosheth calls himself "a dead dog" before David (2 Samuel 9:8). In the Lachish letters, written by an officer in Judah about 589 BC, the writer says, "Who is your servant but a dog, that my lord should remember his servant?" Hazael means: how could a mere servant become a conqueror? But "this great thing" can also be heard as the throne itself. Elisha's answer, "king over Aram," shows that he knows what Hazael is thinking.

a: he took the bed covering, dipped it in water, and laid it across his face
t: A murder, or a cooling cloth?
p: Most read that Hazael smothered the sick king. Assyrian records call Hazael "son of a nobody" who seized the throne.
b: The Hebrew says only "he took," without a name, and "he died." Most readers understand Hazael smothering Ben-hadad with a wet cloth, which would leave no marks. A few have suggested that Ben-hadad himself took a cooling cloth and died of his fever. An inscription of Shalmaneser III of Assyria says: "Hadad-ezer passed away; Hazael, son of a nobody, took the throne." "Son of a nobody" was the Assyrian way to describe a usurper with no royal father. That fits a coup better than a natural death, and it suggests that "Ben-hadad" here is Hadad-ezer (see the note on 6:24).

a: Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat became king over Judah
p: Now both kingdoms have a king called Jehoram (or Joram). The Hebrew uses both spellings for each.
b: Judah's Jehoram was the son of good King Jehoshaphat and the husband of Ahab's daughter Athaliah (8:18). For a few years the two kingdoms had brothers-in-law of the same name on their thrones; on the two spellings and where the Hebrew uses each, see the note on 3:1. The phrase "Jehoshaphat being king of Judah" may point to a co-regency, in which Jehoram began to rule while his father was still alive (see the variant). That would also explain why 1:17 dates Israel's Jehoram by Judah's Jehoram while 3:1 dates him by Jehoshaphat.

a: because his wife was a daughter of Ahab
p: Jehoshaphat married his son to Ahab's daughter Athaliah. Kings blames the match for Judah's slide toward Baal.
b: The alliance between Jehoshaphat and Ahab (1 Kings 22:4, 22:44) was sealed by this marriage. For Kings it was a disaster: Jehoram "walked in the road of Israel's kings," and his son Ahaziah followed (8:27). After Ahaziah's death his mother Athaliah would seize Judah's throne and kill the royal heirs (11:1). Chronicles adds that Jehoram killed all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4), and that a letter "from Elijah the prophet" condemned him (2 Chronicles 21:12–15). That letter is a puzzle, since Elijah seems to have been taken up already in Jehoshaphat's lifetime (3:11); some think Elijah wrote it before he went, others that Chronicles credits Elijah's school.

a: He had told David he would give him a lamp
p: The "lamp" is a living heir on David's throne. God's promise to David keeps Judah alive when its kings fail.
b: A burning lamp in a house meant someone still lived there. Kings uses the picture for the line of David: Solomon's son would keep one tribe "so that a lamp will burn for David my servant before me always in Jerusalem" (1 Kings 11:36), and "because of David" God gave Abijam a lamp (1 Kings 15:4). The promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–16 holds even when a king is as bad as Jehoram. Psalm 132:17 says, "I have set a lamp in order for my anointed one." Chronicles here speaks of "the covenant he had made with David" (2 Chronicles 21:7). The theme returns at the book's end, when David's heir is freed from prison (25:27–30).
r: 1 Kings 11:36; 1 Kings 15:4; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 2 Samuel 21:17; Psalm 132:17; 2 Chronicles 21:7; 25:27–30

a: During his reign Edom revolted out from under Judah's hand
p: Isaac had told Esau that one day he would break his brother's yoke from his neck (Genesis 27:40).
b: Edom had been under Judah since David (2 Samuel 8:14), with a deputy in Jehoshaphat's day (1 Kings 22:47). Its revolt now fulfills Isaac's words to Esau: "But when you break loose, / you will tear his yoke off your neck" (Genesis 27:40). Edom would fight Judah on and off for centuries (14:7; 16:6), and its betrayal at Jerusalem's fall made it a byword among the prophets (Obadiah 10–14). Chronicles gives a theological reason: Libnah revolted "because he had left the LORD, the God of his ancestors" (2 Chronicles 21:10).

a: Joram went across to Zair
p: The verse is one of the hardest in Kings. It seems Joram broke out of an Edomite trap by night, but his army fled.
b: Zair is unknown; some suggest Zoar at the south end of the Dead Sea, or Zior near Hebron (Joshua 15:54), or Seir, Edom's hill country. Chronicles reads "with his commanders" instead (see the variant). The Hebrew is unclear about who surrounded whom: either Edom surrounded Joram and he broke out at night, striking them and the chariot commanders, or Joram and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him. Either way the result was a retreat: "the people fled to their tents," that is, went home, and Edom stayed free (8:22).

a: Then Libnah also revolted
p: Libnah was a town of Judah's western lowland, near Philistia. Its revolt shows Judah losing ground on two sides.
b: Libnah lay in the Shephelah, the hills between Judah and the Philistine coast, and was one of the towns given to the priests (Joshua 21:13). Its revolt probably means it went over to the Philistines. Chronicles tells of a Philistine and Arab raid in Jehoram's reign that carried off his wives and sons, all but the youngest, Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 21:16–17; 22:1). Libnah appears again when Sennacherib attacks it (19:8), and as the hometown of two queen mothers (23:31; 24:18).

a: Athaliah daughter of Omri king of Israel
p: Hebrew bat, "daughter," can mean granddaughter or female descendant. 8:18 calls her a daughter of Ahab.
b: Since 8:18 says Jehoram's wife was "a daughter of Ahab," most readers take "daughter of Omri" to mean "of Omri's house." Some historians, noting the dates, argue that she was in fact Omri's daughter and Ahab's sister, raised at Ahab's court. Either way she brought the house of Omri into David's line. Her name, Athaliah, means "the LORD is exalted," another Omride name honoring the LORD (compare 3:1). Her story continues in chapter 11.

a: Ramoth-gilead
p: Israel and Judah fight Aram again at the town where Ahab died. The wounding of Joram sets up Jehu's coup.
b: Ramoth-gilead, east of the Jordan, was the border fortress that Ahab and Jehoshaphat tried to retake and where Ahab was killed (1 Kings 22:3–37). A generation later their sons, Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, fight Hazael for it. Joram is wounded and goes to recover at Jezreel, the royal winter town in the valley. His absence from the army at Ramoth is the moment when a prophet anoints Jehu, one of his commanders (9:1–14). The Tel Dan stele, probably set up by Hazael, claims that he killed both kings (see 9:24–28).
